strengths: UNOT offers a useful combination of neural operators, synthetic adversarial training, and Sinkhorn bootstrapping. Extending amortized dual prediction to variable-resolution grids without requiring fully converged training labels is a meaningful contribution.

The empirical transfer results are strong. Table 4 reports roughly 1.3–2.8% transport-cost errors across six dataset pairings, substantially improving on Gaussian initialization and outperforming MNIST-trained Meta OT outside MNIST. The resolution sweeps and spherical experiments broaden the evidence.

Evaluation extends beyond scalar costs: Figures 18–19 examine marginal feasibility, and Table 6 reports improved barycenter accuracy. Runtime measurements include the network forward pass and demonstrate substantial savings under the reported conditions.

Proposition 5 provides a useful contraction-based justification for the bootstrapping residual. Detailed architecture descriptions, hyperparameters, pseudocode, and a code/weights link also support understanding and reproduction.
weaknesses: The theoretical bridge to resolution invariance uses inconsistent dual conventions. For Equation (3), the discrete plan is Π_ij = μ_i ν_j exp((f_i + g_j − C_ij)/ε). Thus the learned Sinkhorn scaling potential ε log v_j equals g_j + ε log ν_j, up to a constant. Proposition 2 concerns canonically extended KL-dual potentials, so its convergence guarantee does not directly cover the implemented target. The missing change of variables and discretization normalization affect a central theoretical claim.

The generator universality theorem does not establish universality of the implemented generator. Theorem 3 requires equal input/output dimensions and Lip(NN) < λ, whereas Appendix C uses a 200-dimensional latent for two 64×64 outputs and explicitly does not enforce the Lipschitz constraint. The manifold hypothesis does not repair this gap. Even full support for an idealized generator would not establish coverage or uniform accuracy after finite adversarial training.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of the proposed training mechanism. Comparisons against a fixed random generator, non-adversarial synthetic training, and an FNO trained with Meta OT's dual objective would clarify whether adversarial generation and bootstrapping provide distinct benefits. Table 4 establishes transfer performance, but its different training distributions prevent attributing that advantage to the architecture or loss.

The strongest speed claims use time to reach 1% error relative to a known reference cost, which is unavailable as a stopping criterion in deployment. The appendix supplies marginal-error curves, but not corresponding runtime comparisons at common feasibility or duality-gap tolerances. End-to-end comparisons against efficiently implemented competing initializers are also needed before the state-of-the-art speed claim is convincing.

The downstream algorithms contain substantive mathematical issues. Equation (11) omits the derivative of the outer Sinkhorn divergence's self-transport term. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to updated probability masses; a nonuniform optimum is generally not a fixed point of this update, even when its projected gradient vanishes. These formulas need correction and reconciliation with the implementation before the geometry experiments are reproducible. The GeONet superiority claim also rests on a very limited qualitative comparison.

Several objective definitions require correction. Equation (1) subtracts KL divergence, whereas the stated entropic dual corresponds to adding it. Algorithm 1 returns only ⟨C,Π⟩ while using the notation assigned elsewhere to the full regularized objective. The sign is readily correctable, but the distinction between transport cost and regularized objective must be explicit in the reported errors and Sinkhorn-divergence calculations.
